content.title: Close a simple timestep balance
content.scenario: A 10 mm rainfall timestep produces 1 mm ET, 3 mm outlet runoff, no leakage, and increases all modeled stores by 6 mm.

steps.text: Keep every term as catchment depth; no area conversion is needed.
Compute accounted water: 1 mm + 3 mm + 0 mm + 6 mm = 10 mm.
Residual = input − accounted water = 10 mm − 10 mm = 0 mm.

content.result: The timestep closes exactly at the precision shown.
content.interpretation: A nonzero residual should trigger store-by-store inspection before calibration or parameter changes.

content.title: Runoff changes after an ET refactor
content.observed_behavior: Total ET is nearly unchanged, but infiltration excess increases.
content.conditions: The ET calls were moved, cached soil deficit was retained, or units were converted at a different point.
content.candidate_causes: Changed process ordering; stale soil deficit; PET rate/depth mismatch; routing state reset.
content.reasoning: Routing cannot alter partitioned volume at its source. A stale or differently timed deficit directly changes partitioning capacity, so inspect ET ordering and deficit recomputation first.
content.recommended_action: Compare rainfall ET, retention ET, soil ET, deficit, infiltration, excess, and soil storage immediately before and after the refactor.

content.title: Plausible hydrograph, wrong reservoir timescale
content.observed_behavior: Baseflow shape looks smooth but drains much faster than expected.
content.conditions: A coefficient documented per hour was applied as if it were per second, or an initial storage fraction was treated as metres.
content.candidate_causes: Unit mismatch; wrong exponential flag; incorrect threshold; timestep change without parameter conversion.
content.reasoning: Routing can delay a flux but cannot repair a reservoir outlet computed on the wrong timescale. Inspect the reservoir law and coefficient units before tuning routing.
content.recommended_action: Record storage, maximum storage, threshold, coefficient, exponent, exponential flag, and timestep units together for both soil and groundwater.

inline.text: Changing GIUH ordinates or Nash parameters redistributes water in time. It cannot correct a systematic excess created by partitioning, forcing conversion, or reservoir leakage.

content.title: A pulse vanishes after one update
content.observed_behavior: A multi-timestep GIUH response appears only in the rainfall timestep.
content.conditions: Ordinates contain delayed weights, but later queue values are zero.
content.candidate_causes: Queue reinitialization; malformed ordinates; wrong number of ordinates; output read before state update.
content.reasoning: Delayed ordinates place water in future queue slots. If those slots vanish, persistent routing state—not partitioning—is the first suspect.
content.recommended_action: Log the complete GIUH queue before addition, after addition, and after shifting across several dry timesteps; also verify the ordinate sum.

content.title: Mass balance closes, but the hydrograph is late
content.observed_behavior: Cumulative input and output close within tolerance, yet peak runoff arrives several timesteps too late.
content.conditions: Forcing conversion and total partitioned volumes match a reference run.
content.candidate_causes: GIUH ordinate shift; Nash K or N mismatch; routing state carried from another run; timestamp convention mismatch.
content.reasoning: Closed mass balance rules out lost or created water but not mistimed water. Because partitioned volumes agree, routing and clock alignment are more likely than infiltration parameters.
content.recommended_action: Compare direct, lateral, and groundwater components by timestep; inspect GIUH queue and Nash stores; then verify BMI current-time advancement.
